study.title: 1 John 1 The Word of life, communion and confession of sin
study.overview: The chapter presents the apostolic testimony about Jesus Christ as the Word of life, eternal and manifested in the flesh. This announcement is not just information: he calls the reader for communion with the Father and with the Son, producing complete joy. Then John exposes the central moral message: God is light, so that communion with him does not match life in darkness. The chapter concludes by showing that authentic Christian life does not deny sin, but confesses it; purification comes through the blood of Jesus Christ, and denying sin makes God a liar in our eyes.

outline.title: The Apostolic Testimony on the Word of Life
outline.explanation: John presents what was heard, seen and touched concerning Jesus. The focus is on the historical and personal reality of the manifestation of eternal life in Christ, to lead readers to communion with the apostles, with the Father and with the Son, and for joy to be complete.

outline.title: God is light and true communion demands walking in the light
outline.explanation: The message received from Jesus is that God is light and there is no darkness in him. So say that you have fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie. The walk in the light produces communion with other believers and is linked to the purification carried out by the blood of Jesus.

outline.title: The reality of sin and the need for confession
outline.explanation: John rejects every claim that he has no sin or not sin. The denial of sin deceives the person, contradicts the truth and calls God a liar. The right way is to confess sins, trusting in the faithful and righteous character of God to forgive and purify.

study.context: The epistle was written as an apostolic witness against any version of the Christian faith that separated communion with God from the reality of the incarnate Christ, from holiness and from the honest confession of sin. By the notes provided, the writing also dialogues with teachings that denied the gravity of sin and the bond between true faith and holy life. The prologue has a poetic form and recalls the prologue of the gospel of John, but here the goal is pastoral and exhortation: to proclaim, correct and lead to communion.
study.theology: The chapter teaches incarnational Christology: Jesus is the Word of life, eternal and revealed to the apostles, not an abstract idea. He also teaches that communion with God is inseparable from practical holiness, for God is light. The doctrine of sin is direct and realistic: even believers need to recognize their guilt and dependence on God. Purification comes not from denial or human effort, but from the blood of Jesus Christ. Confession does not buy forgiveness; it is the humble way by which the sinner stands before the faithful and just God, who forgives on the basis of the work of Christ. Thus grace does not relativize sin; it exposes him, confesses him and treats him with forgiveness and purification.

scholarViews.insight: The apostolic testimony is presented as an invitation for readers to enter into the same communion with the Father and the Son; the expression "we" includes the apostles as eyewitnesses of the incarnation.
True Christian life does not combine communion with God and permanence in darkness; walking in light involves real communion with God and with our brothers and sisters.
To confess sins is to humble yourself before God, recognizing guilt and helplessness, and trust that he forgives because of the work of Christ.

questions: What changes in the reading of the chapter when we realize that John insists on real testimony - to hear, see and touch - about Jesus Christ?
In what practical ways can anyone say that he has fellowship with God, but still walking in darkness?
Why is the honest confession of sin more consistent with the Christian faith than to deny one's own guilt?
study.practice: This week, take a daily time to examine your life in the light of 1 John 1. Name concrete sins before God, without excuses or generalities, and thank for forgiveness in Christ. Then try to live in a way consistent with the light: restore what is necessary, abandon hidden habits and strengthen communion with the church, because walking in the light also appears in the relationship with the brothers.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow to safely determine broader historical details, exact date, specific recipients or context external to the chapter itself. There are also limitations in Tyndale's notes for verses 1 and 2, which appear truncated; therefore, the study used only the clearly available content and avoided widening beyond what was provided.
